item.research_question: How do temperature, strain rate, and grain size influence the micromechanical behavior, phase transformation, and deformation mechanisms of the Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 high-entropy alloy?
item.processing_route: Molecular dynamics simulation using LAMMPS with EAM potential functions; model size 30a × 30a × 30a (54,000 atoms); relaxed 50fs under NPT; tensile strain of 0.35 along Y direction at temperatures of 77, 300, 700, and 1000 K and strain rates of 1 × 10^9, 5 × 10^9, 1 × 10^10, 3 × 10^10, and 5 × 10^10 s^-1 under NVT ensemble; grain size variation via Voronoi structure method (10 × 10 × 10 nm^3 models with 2, 4, 6, and 8 grains).
item.test_conditions: Temperatures: 77 K, 300 K, 700 K, 1000 K; Strain rates: 1 × 10^9 s^-1 to 5 × 10^10 s^-1; Strain: up to 0.35; Grain sizes: varied by number of grains (2, 4, 6, 8) in 10 nm^3 models.
key_findings: The alloy undergoes a phase transition from BCC to FCC during tensile loading, with FCC reaching a maximum content of about 51% at 0.2 strain.
At high temperatures (e.g., 1000 K) and low strain rates (1 × 10^9 s^-1), grain boundary slip is the dominant deformation mechanism.
At low temperatures (e.g., 77 K) and high strain rates (1 × 10^10 s^-1), dislocation slip replaces grain boundary slip as the dominant mechanism.
Dislocation density at 77 K was 4.6 × 10^17 m^-2 (1 × 10^9 s^-1) and 5 × 10^17 m^-2 (1 × 10^10 s^-1), while at 1000 K it was 2.5 × 10^16 m^-2 and 1 × 10^17 m^-2 respectively.
The elastic modulus at 300 K and 1 × 10^10 s^-1 was calculated as 116.7 GPa.
Ultimate strength increases with increasing strain rate, showing a positive correlation.
An inverse Hall–Petch relationship was observed where strength decreased when grain size became too small (e.g., 6 and 8 grains had lower strength than 4 grains).
The alloy exhibits a transition from single crystal to polycrystal during the tensile process.
item.mechanism: At high temperatures, intensified thermal motion causes atoms at grain boundaries to break away and become disordered, leading to grain boundary slip. At low temperatures and high strain rates, dislocations are generated within grains, slip, and accumulate at boundaries to form knots, increasing resistance to deformation. The inverse Hall–Petch effect occurs because small grain sizes hinder dislocation movement and entanglement within grains and make grain boundaries more prone to breakdown.
item.limitations: The study is based on molecular dynamics simulations which may not fully capture all experimental conditions; the specific potential function used was fitted by Zhou et al. and verified against limited experimental data.
item.future_work: The study offers a new compositional window for additive manufactured lightweight high-strength materials and provides theoretical guidance for improving service performance and structural regulation of HEAs.
quotes: The Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 alloy changes from a single crystal to a polycrystal during the tensile process, and the transition of the Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 (at.%) high-entropy alloy from the BCC phase to the FCC phase occurs.

At high temperatures and low strain rates, grain boundary slip is the main deformation mechanism, and at low temperatures and high strain rates, dislocation slip replaces grain boundary slip as the dominant deformation mechanism.
When the grain size is too small, the strength of the alloy decreases, which does not satisfy the fine grain strengthening theory and shows an inverse Hall–Petch relationship.
